content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In popular Christian teaching, lamp oil is most commonly interpreted as a symbol of the Holy Spirit — the inward, divine presence or empowering that cannot be borrowed or transferred and that sustains the believer's light/witness. In the Parable of the Ten Virgins this is typically preached as the indwelling Spirit (or, closely related, genuine spiritual life produced by the Spirit) that distinguishes true readiness for Christ's return from mere outward profession.", "primary_basis": ["Matthew 25:1-13 (Parable of the Ten Virgins — the central lamp-oil text)", "Zechariah 4:1-6 (the golden lampstand fed by oil, interpreted 'not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit')", "Exodus 27:20-21 (pure oil to keep the tabernacle lamps burning continually)", "1 Samuel 16:13 (anointing oil linked with the Spirit coming upon David)", "Acts 10:38 (God 'anointed' Jesus with the Holy Spirit and power)", "1 John 2:20, 27 ('anointing' from the Holy One, commonly connected to the oil/Spirit link)", "Psalm 45:7 / Hebrews 1:9 ('oil of gladness' associated with divine anointing)"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Good works, deeds of love, or the fruit of genuine discipleship — the classic Augustinian/patristic reading of the wise virgins' oil, sometimes tied to Matthew 5:14-16 (light shining through good works).", "basis": ["Matthew 25:1-13", "Matthew 5:14-16", "Augustine's sermons on the Ten Virgins; echoed in medieval and some later exegesis"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Saving faith or grace — Reformation-era and later Protestant readings take the oil as true, living faith (or God's grace) versus empty profession.", "basis": ["Matthew 25:1-13", "Ephesians 2:8-9 (grace/faith framing)", "Luther, Calvin, and later Protestant commentary traditions"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Spiritual preparedness/watchfulness with no fixed allegorical referent — many modern academic commentators argue the oil is simply a narrative device meaning 'readiness' for the delayed Parousia and should not be allegorized.", "basis": ["Matthew 25:1-13 read in context of Matthew 24:36-25:46 (watchfulness discourse)", "Standard critical commentaries on Matthew (e.g., Davies-Allison, France, Hagner note caution against allegorizing)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "The Word of God / knowledge of God as that which fuels the believer's light (lamp = Word, Psalm 119:105, so oil = what keeps the Word alive in the heart).", "basis": ["Psalm 119:105", "Proverbs 6:23", "Matthew 25:1-13"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Personal righteousness or a testimony/relationship with Christ that cannot be borrowed — a reading emphasized in some traditions (notably Latter-day Saint teaching) and some evangelical preaching, focusing on the non-transferability of the oil.", "basis": ["Matthew 25:1-13 (the wise cannot share their oil)", "LDS teaching (e.g., Spencer W. Kimball's 'drop by drop' exposition)"], "prominence": "minority"}], "has_settled_consensus": false, "confidence": "medium", "notes": "There is a recognizable dominant strand — oil = Holy Spirit — that prevails in popular, devotional, Pentecostal/charismatic, and much evangelical teaching, grounded in the broader biblical association of anointing oil with the Spirit. However, this is not a settled scholarly consensus: the history of interpretation is genuinely divided (good works in Augustine and much patristic/medieval exegesis; faith/grace in Reformation exegesis; Holy Spirit in much modern preaching), and a large share of modern critical commentators decline to allegorize the oil at all, treating it as a figure for readiness. So the honest picture is: dominant popular meaning = Holy Spirit; academic consensus = deliberately non-allegorical 'preparedness'; historical alternatives remain live. Confidence is medium because prominence rankings among the alternatives vary by tradition and era."}
